power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Will members of 12-step recovery groups oppose the use of GLP-1 agonists for addiction?

text.text: The integration of pharmacotherapy into abstinence-oriented recovery communities has historically been met with friction.
However, a new dynamic may be emerging with the rise of GLP-1 agonists (e.g., semaglutide).

While robust clinical trial data for GLP-1s regarding the treatment of substance use disorders remains unclear, these new medications are being adopted off-label by innovators in abstinence-oriented treatment facilities and selectively within the 12-step recovery community.
This commentary provides an analysis of this phenomenon through the application of Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations theory.

We argue that unlike previous medications which faced medication stigma for their psychoactive properties, it may be possible that GLP-1s are being met with less resistance from the recovery community because their mechanism of action is culturally congruent with the 12-step goal of relieving the mental obsession of addiction.
We posit that this new phenomenon represents a practice-based evidence signal that deserves attention; perhaps the 12-step recovery community is not as anti-medication as once thought.
Abstinence-oriented 12-step mutual help groups remain the most widely accessed form of support for substance use disorders (SUD) in the United States.

Approximately three to four million Americans attend Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) in any given year, with millions more participating in fellowships focused on other addictions. 1, 2 These communities can substantially influence the adoption of addiction pharmacotherapy in everyday treatment.
text.formatted: Approximately three to four million Americans attend Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) in any given year, with millions more participating in fellowships focused on other addictions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> These communities can substantially influence the adoption of addiction pharmacotherapy in everyday treatment.

text.text: The relationship between abstinence-oriented recovery fellowships and addiction pharmacotherapy is often characterized as adversarial. 3 For decades, methadone has faced skepticism within 12-step groups as "an easier, softer way" that maintains physiological dependence rather than achieving the spiritual transformation central to these fellowships. 4 For their part, some prescribers of addiction pharmacotherapy will not refer patients to 12-step mutual help groups because they see them as anti-medication, anti-science or both. 4 Attitudes toward pharmacotherapy vary across 12-step fellowships (e.g., Narcotics Anonymous vs.
text.formatted: The relationship between abstinence-oriented recovery fellowships and addiction pharmacotherapy is often characterized as adversarial. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> For decades, methadone has faced skepticism within 12-step groups as "an easier, softer way" that maintains physiological dependence rather than achieving the spiritual transformation central to these fellowships. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> For their part, some prescribers of addiction pharmacotherapy will not refer patients to 12-step mutual help groups because they see them as anti-medication, anti-science or both. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> Attitudes toward pharmacotherapy vary across 12-step fellowships (e.g., Narcotics Anonymous vs.

text.text: AA), local groups within the same fellowship, and within different cultural contexts. 2 The emergence of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists as potential treatments for SUD again raises the question of whether recovery fellowships will accept or reject pharmacotherapy.
text.formatted: AA), local groups within the same fellowship, and within different cultural contexts. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> The emergence of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists as potential treatments for SUD again raises the question of whether recovery fellowships will accept or reject pharmacotherapy.

text.text: Perhaps surprisingly, the history of medications in mutual help groups is not uniformly one of sustained resistance.
Antidepressant use was once discouraged in AA, viewed by some members as incompatible with authentic sobriety.

By the turn of the century, their use had become largely unremarkable within 12-step groups. 3 Similarly, medications for alcohol use disorder (e.g., naltrexone, acamprosate) eventually achieved at least some degree of acceptance within AA.
text.formatted: By the turn of the century, their use had become largely unremarkable within 12-step groups. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> Similarly, medications for alcohol use disorder (e.g., naltrexone, acamprosate) eventually achieved at least some degree of acceptance within AA.

text.text: These medications appear to have gained acceptance as sustained opposition diminished.

Naltrexone and antidepressants provoked no long-term organized resistance, whereas methadone faced persistent opposition that became institutionalized. 4 GLP-1 receptor agonists may follow the path of antidepressants and naltrexone rather than that of methadone.
text.formatted: Naltrexone and antidepressants provoked no long-term organized resistance, whereas methadone faced persistent opposition that became institutionalized. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> GLP-1 receptor agonists may follow the path of antidepressants and naltrexone rather than that of methadone.

text.text: Health-claims data show increasing GLP-1 agonist prescribing among patients with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity and co-occurring alcohol use disorder, 5 and early signals suggest that these medications may be finding acceptance within abstinence-oriented recovery fellowships with surprisingly little resistance.
text.formatted: Health-claims data show increasing GLP-1 agonist prescribing among patients with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity and co-occurring alcohol use disorder, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> and early signals suggest that these medications may be finding acceptance within abstinence-oriented recovery fellowships with surprisingly little resistance.

text.text: With prospective trials underway 6 and reviews identifying GLP-1-based therapies as an emerging treatment option for alcohol use disorder, 7 clinicians need to understand whether members of AA and other mutual help groups will accept these medications.
text.formatted: With prospective trials underway <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> and reviews identifying GLP-1-based therapies as an emerging treatment option for alcohol use disorder, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> clinicians need to understand whether members of AA and other mutual help groups will accept these medications.

text.text: A residential facility with 12-step philosophical roots has prescribed GLP-1 medications off-label to over 440 patients using a structured protocol including informed consent and clinical follow-up. 8 The clinicians developed their approach from available preclinical, retrospective, and clinical data and their participation in a formal trial evaluating these medications in opioid use disorder. 9 A similar pilot program is underway at a second nonprofit residential treatment center.
text.formatted: A residential facility with 12-step philosophical roots has prescribed GLP-1 medications off-label to over 440 patients using a structured protocol including informed consent and clinical follow-up. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> The clinicians developed their approach from available preclinical, retrospective, and clinical data and their participation in a formal trial evaluating these medications in opioid use disorder. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> A similar pilot program is underway at a second nonprofit residential treatment center.

text.text: The physicians leading these efforts are themselves in recovery from addiction and are supporters of a 12-step approach, and the program emerged partly from observing outcomes among AA members taking these medications for metabolic indications.

According to Rogers' diffusion of innovations theory, a primary determinant of an innovation's adoption is its perceived compatibility with a community's existing values. 10 A foundational belief of 12-step recovery is the promise of a new freedom in which the obsession to use substances has been lifted through a spiritual awakening from working the 12 steps.
text.formatted: According to Rogers' diffusion of innovations theory, a primary determinant of an innovation's adoption is its perceived compatibility with a community's existing values. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> A foundational belief of 12-step recovery is the promise of a new freedom in which the obsession to use substances has been lifted through a spiritual awakening from working the 12 steps.

text.text: In practice, this has often meant that the spiritual transformation must be maintained without the continued use of the drug of choice or a substitute acting on the same receptors. 4 Opioid agonist therapies relieve craving through continued opioid receptor activation, which may conflict with how some 12-step group members conceptualize recovery despite the medications' effectiveness.
text.formatted: In practice, this has often meant that the spiritual transformation must be maintained without the continued use of the drug of choice or a substitute acting on the same receptors. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> Opioid agonist therapies relieve craving through continued opioid receptor activation, which may conflict with how some 12-step group members conceptualize recovery despite the medications' effectiveness.

text.text: GLP-1 agonists may achieve compatibility precisely because of this critical distinction.
Patients report that the mental obsession is silenced with these medications.
GLP-1 agonists activate GLP-1 receptors, without substituting an agonist at the opioid receptors targeted by methadone or buprenorphine.
Members may therefore perceive their effects as more closely aligned with the 12-step ideal of the obsession being lifted.
Consequently, the characterization of abstinence-oriented recovery as categorically anti-medication may be overdrawn.

These communities have eventually learned to tolerate medications in the past as the trajectories of antidepressants and naltrexone suggest. 3 We argue that members' resistance to pharmacotherapy may depend on perceived alignment with 12-step recovery values.
text.formatted: These communities have eventually learned to tolerate medications in the past as the trajectories of antidepressants and naltrexone suggest. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> We argue that members' resistance to pharmacotherapy may depend on perceived alignment with 12-step recovery values.

text.text: If this early receptivity persists, members of the global 12-step mutual-help network may increasingly adopt GLP-1 agonists, consistent with Rogers' prediction that value compatibility influences adoption.
